headline_marked: Highly Educated [[Training AI]] That May Replace Them
headline: Highly Educated Training AI That May Replace Them
summary: AI companies are hiring professionals to transfer their judgment and skills to machines, even as those systems could eventually perform their jobs.
details: AI companies are increasingly hiring highly educated individuals to train AI systems, effectively transferring their years of developed judgment and expertise to machines that may eventually replace them. This practice raises ethical questions about the future of work and the value of human skills in an increasingly automated world.

James Maisiri, who holds a Ph.D. in industrial sociology, was offered a role training an AI to design assessments, teach, and mark essays. Despite the potential for the AI to replace his own future academic career, the offered pay of $37/hour in South Africa, where the national minimum wage is $2/hour and youth unemployment is high, presented a difficult socioeconomic dilemma.

This trend extends beyond academia. Skilled writers are paid to edit AI-generated text, and in India, workers are capturing their daily activities to train humanoid robots that could automate their jobs. The common thread is the extraction of human knowledge and judgment to build AI systems, often at low wages.

For AI companies, there's a clear incentive to leverage the growing pool of educated professionals in regions like Africa, where AI adoption rates are lower but unemployment is high. This allows them to acquire expert knowledge at a lower cost compared to Western societies.

The AI jobs now require more than just data labeling; they demand the transfer of nuanced human judgment. This includes understanding complex concepts, evaluating work, and discerning genuine understanding from memorization – the very skills that define professions like law, medicine, and teaching.

The recruitment process itself is becoming automated. Maisiri was interviewed and assessed by an AI, which then provided feedback on his performance, highlighting a shift in how human talent is evaluated and selected for these new roles.

headline_marked: TiVo to [[charge for commercial skipping]] on your recordings starting November 2
headline: TiVo to charge for commercial skipping on your recordings starting November 2
summary: The popular SkipMode feature, which allows users to bypass commercials with a single button press, will be replaced by a paid add-on service.
details: TiVo is phasing out its long-standing SkipMode feature, which automatically skips commercial breaks on recorded shows. Starting November 2, 2026, this convenience will no longer be part of the standard TiVo service.
The company is introducing a new paid service called Premium Auto Commercial Skip. While the exact pricing is yet to be announced, TiVo will offer a 30-day free trial of this new feature in November.

Existing recordings with SkipMode markers will continue to function normally until the November 2, 2026 deadline. However, new recordings made after this date will not include the free commercial skip data.

This change reflects TiVo's parent company, Xperi's, strategic shift away from hardware manufacturing towards smart-TV operating systems and advertising technology. Automatic commercial skipping has been a key differentiator for TiVo.

The move will require long-time users to decide if the convenience of automatic ad skipping is worth an additional monthly fee, or if they will revert to manual fast-forwarding. TiVo plans to provide more details on the new service soon.
